_doc: THE MERGE QUEUE. The manager SCHEDULES merges; it does not resolve the
conflicts that not scheduling them causes.
⚠️ THIS FILE DID NOT EXIST UNTIL 2026-09-03, AND ITS ABSENCE IS THE POINT.
The day manager ran a merge queue that morning -- it declared an order, it
held sessions at position 2+, it promoted and poked -- and it worked. But it
existed only in that session's context. It was cited to a sub-session as
'the state of record ... created today', and a search of every branch and
every commit in the repo found NOTHING: not on main, not on any ref, not in
history. What existed was docs/runbooks/merge-queue.md, which is prose.
That is the exact failure the operator named on 2026-09-03: 'that's one of
the base functions of what a manager session is supposed to do. That needs
to be canonized. It's not something you take upon yourself in the session.'
A queue held in a session's head dies with that session, and the next
manager re-derives it from scratch -- or does not, and the morning repeats.
MEASURED HARM on the day the queue was invented, which is why it exists:
26 merges to main, 19 of them (73%) touching a shared register, five of
those the manager's own and two of THOSE bare lease heartbeats -- merges
whose entire content is a timestamp. Every one re-conflicted every open PR
touching a register. #10918 went dirty three times; #10923 the moment it
went green. Sessions burned ~16-minute pytest-runs that were void before
they finished.
THE INVARIANT THIS FILE EXISTS TO HOLD, and the one check_manager_scope.py
R8 enforces: AT MOST ONE ENTRY IS REBASING AT A TIME. Two sessions rebasing
against the same moving main is the thundering herd the queue prevents; it
is also the state that looks fine to each session individually, which is why
it needs a check rather than a convention.
PROMOTE AND POKE. A session does not poll. When position 1 lands, the
manager sets the next entry to `rebasing` AND messages that session. An
entry left `waiting` with nothing ahead of it is a session sitting idle for
a promotion nobody sent -- the 46-minute block the operator caught, in a
different costume.
STATES, NEVER COLLAPSED:
waiting   -- in the queue, not yet cleared to rebase. Do NOT rebase.
rebasing  -- cleared, and the ONLY entry that may be. At most one.
green     -- rebased, CI passed, waiting on the manager's merge click.
merged    -- landed. Keep the row until the next manager reads it.
blocked   -- cannot proceed; `blocked_on` says why. NOT `waiting`:
'not my turn' and 'cannot go' are different facts.
⚠️ `green` IS THE STATE THAT COST US. #10923 sat green and mergeable from
11:01:05Z to 11:11Z and the OPERATOR noticed before the mechanism did. The
manager's own 11:04Z sweep timer was enabled, carried next_run_at 11:04:00Z,
and never fired -- no error, no log. A cadence check that graded whether a
sweep was ARMED would have passed straight through that hole, because it WAS
armed. See check_manager_scope.py's R7 note for what is and is not covered.
note: ⚠️ THIS FILE WAS STALE FOR TWELVE HOURS AND THAT IS MY OWN FAILURE, RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY REPAIRED. It read 'queue EMPTY as of 2026-09-08T07:06Z' while I merged roughly nine PRs and ran an eleven-PR HOLD that existed only in my session context and in PR comments. That is MI-102 exactly — a queue run successfully for a day in one session's head, cited as 'the state of record', and found on no branch and in no commit — and a cold successor reading this file would have seen an empty queue and started merging the held PRs. R8 passed throughout, correctly: its one invariant is 'at most one entry rebasing', which an empty list satisfies trivially. A guard that cannot fail on emptiness is not evidence the queue is being kept. STATE 2026-09-08T18:58Z: eleven entries. #11391 is next and everything else is BLOCKED on the hold that protects it. RELEASE THE HOLD the moment #11391 lands, and say so on the PR. WHAT PASSED THROUGH MY QUEUE TODAY AND IS NOT LISTED HERE (the ledger this file should have been carrying): #11403, #11406, #11407, #11412, #11426, #11430, #11433, #11434, #11435 merged BY ME, and #11370, #11384, #11418 self-landed under my hold — twelve, every one verified present in origin/main's PR list rather than recalled. ⚠️ STATE THE POPULATION: main took 94 commits today across roughly 96 distinct PRs, so MOST of today's landings were not mine and this is not a ledger of main. It is a RECONSTRUCTION from my own session record checked against the log, not a contemporaneous record — which is the point. || CORRECTED 19:20Z, AND THE CORRECTION IS THE POINT. I wrote these nine automation rows as `blocked` on my own queue-hold. THAT WAS WRONG AND IT WAS A FALSE BLOCKER. Reading #11431's CI log rather than assuming: guards PASS 53 / FAIL 1 / SKIP 38, the one failure pr-landing-guard, cause R13 -- the branch arms auto-merge while its own committed session-board names somebody else's branch in merge_slot. Measured across all nine: every one arms, not one holds the slot. A bot writes no claim, so this NEVER self-heals and re-running CI is pointless. THE HOLD WAS RELEASED AT 19:00Z AND NOTHING MOVED, which is how I found out. ⚠️ I ALSO MIS-READ THIS ONCE MORE ON THE WAY: I grepped a local guard run for 'FAIL' and reported api-tier-policy as the failing guard. It was not -- that string is that guard's own PLANTED self-test defect, and its last line says 'self-test OK'. Grepping a log for a word and calling it a verdict is the unprovenanced-diagnostic trap this repo has a guard for, committed by the manager, twice in one pass. || THE CLASS IS ALREADY FILED AND I DID NOT FILE A FOURTH ROW. backlog_search returned BL-20260908-R13-MAKES-EVERY-AUTOMATION-PR-WRITE-THE-MERGE-SLOT-SO-MAIN-CAN-NEVER-BE-QUIET at 0.75 overlap (open), beside BL-20260908-R13-MAKES-EVERY-CONCURRENT-ARMED-BRANCH-... and BL-20260908-R13-FORCES-EVERY-SELF-LANDING-BRANCH-TO-REWRITE-ONE-5-LINE-OBJECT-... -- three rows on this guard already. What is NEW here is only the COUNT and the fact that it does not self-heal, and that belongs in the manager's own instrument rather than in a fourth row; this file is where a successor manager looks. Filing another would be the accumulation the repo already complains about.

entries.blocked_on: pr-landing-guard R13 -- NOT the manager hold, which is RELEASED. CORRECTED 19:20Z: I first recorded these as blocked on my queue-hold for #11391 and that was a FALSE BLOCKER, which this repo rates worse than a missing one. MEASURED: #11431's CI `guards` job reads PASS 53 / FAIL 1 / SKIP 38 and the single failure is pr-landing-guard; on that branch's OWN committed docs/claude/session-board.json the merge_slot names `claude/mgr-operator-decisions-1805-20260908`, not itself, so R13 refuses the arming. ALL NINE arm auto-merge and NOT ONE holds the slot on its own branch (measured across all nine), and a bot never writes a claim, so this cannot self-heal and a CI re-run changes nothing. They land only when a manager rebases one and claims the slot for it -- which is what #11426 cost me three rebases to do.
